description: Scripted first consultation after sign-up (docs/ux/F02c). sections.title: What I'm Hearing
sections.body: You've been living with {symptoms} for {duration}, and you said it gets in the way of your days {impact}. You're {age} and {stage}{medClause}. That's a lot to carry, and it makes complete sense that you're tired.

sections.title: The Hypothalamic Connection
sections.body: Think of your hypothalamus as your body's thermostat and sleep clock in one. When estrogen drops after menopause, that thermostat can misfire at night and trigger a sweat. Broken sleep then leaves less energy for the day. So your sweats and your tiredness may share one upstream cause.

sections.title: What This May Mean
body: Low estrogen may be making your temperature control less steady at night.
Your thyroid may be worth a fresh look. I often meet women who are 'in range' on TSH and still don't feel like themselves.
A night-time hormone called prolactin may be out of rhythm, which can affect both sleep and energy.

sections.title: Questions to Ask Your Provider
body: Could my {symptoms} be linked to my hormones changing?
Can we check free T3 and free T4, not just TSH?
Are my hormones and thyroid where they should be at {age}?
Would a morning prolactin test make sense for my sleep?

body.why: Shows if your thyroid hormones are actually reaching your cells.
Confirms where your estrogen levels are now.
Checks if your night-time hormone switches off properly in the morning.
Blood sugar swings can also cause night sweats.
Helps your hormones work at the cell level.

sections.title: What You Can Do Now
body: Keep your bedroom cool (around 60–67°F) and fully dark.
Put screens away at dusk. Blue light delays your sleep hormone.
Have a light, early dinner so digestion isn't working overnight.
Get 20 minutes of morning daylight to reset your body clock.
